rates.label: Paper
rates.note: The paper in a thousand square feet of combined board (liners and medium, the medium's take-up included), not a single paper grade's price; prices waste board (trim, shear, rejects), which is combined board.

rates.label: Machine time
rates.note: Bottleneck shadow price of corrugator time (the post: more than $1,200 an hour); prices downtime, the speed gap and the run time shear and rejects consumed.

rates.label: Board contribution margin
rates.note: Not in the post. Prices the board not made; until it is set every contribution figure reads 'margin not set', never $0.

rates.label: Side-trim target
rates.note: The owner's side-trim target (targets.json, issue #101); trim points over it are the trim lever. 3.25% is the flag, 2.75% a home run.

assumptions.label: Annual volume per machine
assumptions.note: The post's 3.6M MSF a year across two machines.

cfg.long_note: Over several days these whole dollars, added shift by shift, can read off the same quantities priced at once in cents, which the formulas and receipts state; over the whole record the widest gap measured is about twenty-five dollars, on a month's waste recorded.

input.ptd_label: 4-4-5 P2 to date through Mon 14 Sep
input.speeds_note: Two speeds, never one definition: the speed lever is each grade's trailing-year baseline (targets.json), and the required speed, 675 ft/min at 10% downtime (rates.json, the post), converts machine minutes to MSF not made and is no lever.
input.method_note: Each lever is its gap to its band in targets.json, summed over the shifts of the window: a shift inside its band adds nothing, and the cost inside the bands is shown apart, at standard, outside the total. A yearly figure is this period's rate, period-to-date dollars per production day x the post's production days a year, never a shift's or a day's own; for all shifts it is each shift's period-to-date rate added up, so the shifts' yearly figures add to it. These name where to look and whom to ask; they never prescribe a machine adjustment.
